planting.note: Set divisions or container plants out in spring once soil has warmed, in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade to full shade.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist to slightly dry soil in a shaded woodland bed, spacing clumps roughly a foot and a half apart. This Appalachian botanical variety carries deep burgundy-purple maple-shaped foliage that holds its color through the growing season, unlike the plain-green typical form of the species, and sends up airy sprays of small white flowers in late summer. It is slow to establish but long-lived and largely untroubled by deer; divide congested clumps in early spring every three to four years to keep the foliage dense.

planting.note: Set rhizome divisions in fall (or very early spring) into saturated, mucky soil so roots knit in before the growing season begins.

directions: Plant rhizomes at the margin of a pond, ditch, or rain garden where soil stays saturated or sits under a few inches of standing water; this is the glacial-marsh and prairie-pothole segregate of blue flag iris, ranging across the upper Midwest rather than the southeastern wet woods favored by the typical variety. Lavender-blue flowers with a yellow-and-white signal patch open in early summer above stiff, sword-like foliage that gives water gardens strong vertical structure. Clumps spread gradually and are easiest to divide in fall; keep the rhizomes from ever drying out, since unlike bearded irises this species has no drought tolerance.
